2027-07-29.title: Thursday of the tenth week after Pentecost · Martha, Mary and Lazarus of Bethany
readings: Let mutual love continue: do not neglect hospitality to strangers
Martha welcomes Jesus into her home, and Mary sits at his feet
2027-07-29.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Tenth Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam prints, in bold, Martha, Mary and Lazarus of Bethany (ബഥനിയിലെ മർത്തായും മറിയവും ലാസറും), the friends of Jesus whose home at Bethany received him. Luke does not name their village; John does, and the Church has long read the two Gospels together.
2027-07-29.verse: Mary has chosen the better part, which will not be taken away from her.
theo: The letter to the Hebrews ends with plain, practical love, and the first words are the oldest rule of the household: “Let mutual love continue. Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by doing that some have entertained angels without knowing it.” The writer is thinking of Abraham and Sarah at the oaks of Mamre, who ran out to three travellers in the noon heat, brought water and bread and a calf, and found that they had received God's own messengers. The letter goes on: remember those in prison as if you were in prison with them; let marriage be honoured by all; be content with what you have, “for he has said, ‘I will never leave you or forsake you.’” Then comes the confident cry of the one who has nothing and fears nothing: “The Lord is my helper; I will not be afraid. What can anyone do to me?” A home where love is steady, where the stranger is welcome and the poor are not forgotten, is a small Church. It is such a home that the Gospel puts before us today.

“Now as they went on their way, he entered a certain village, where a woman named Martha welcomed him into her home.” Luke says that Martha was the host, the one who opened the door, and we should not forget that before we hear her scolded. The Church has sometimes been unfair to Martha. She did what the Letter to the Hebrews asks: she welcomed a traveller, and she wanted the best for him. Her fault was not in serving; it was in being “worried and distracted by many things.” Her sister Mary “sat at the Lord's feet and listened to what he was saying,” the place of a disciple at the feet of a teacher; Saul of Tarsus was brought up “at the feet of Gamaliel”. That Jesus accepts a woman in the disciple's place is itself a quiet revolution. When Martha asks him to send Mary to help, he does not rebuke her harshly; he calls her name twice, as one calls someone dear: “Martha, Martha, you are worried and distracted by many things; there is need of only one thing. Mary has chosen the better part, which will not be taken away from her.”

John fills in the rest of the picture. He names the village, Bethany, “the village of Mary and her sister Martha,” about two miles from Jerusalem, and he tells us in a single sentence how the Lord regarded this house: “Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.” When Lazarus died, it was Martha who ran to meet the Lord on the road, and it was to Martha that he spoke the words that every funeral still repeats: “I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live, and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die. Do you believe this?” And Martha answered with a confession as great as Peter's: “Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God, the one coming into the world.” Then Mary came and fell at his feet, Jesus began to weep, and Lazarus was called out of the tomb. At a supper in the same house some days later Martha was serving again, without complaint now, and Mary anointed his feet with costly perfume until “the house was filled with the fragrance.” The sisters who seem so different are two halves of one discipleship. Mary of Bethany should not be confused with Mary Magdalene, whom the Church remembered on 22 July.

The Church needs both houses of Bethany. Without Martha there would be no table, no school, no hospital, no one to open the door in the monsoon night; without Mary the table would have nothing to serve, for the one thing needed is to know who is sitting at it. Archbishop Mar Ivanios founded Bethany Ashram in 1919, and its name recalls the house at Bethany, a place where welcome and prayer belong together. In our own homes the lesson is easy to apply. In Kerala no visitor comes to the door without being offered water at least, and in the rains a traveller sheltering on the veranda is a guest of God. But when the guest is Jesus himself, hospitality begins with listening. At the Holy Qurbono the two halves of Bethany meet: first we sit at his feet to hear the Word, and then we are brought to his table, where he serves us himself with his own Body and Blood.
outline: Ask: when the Lord comes to my house, am I busy for him or with him?
Hebrews 13: love, hospitality to strangers, content with what we have.
Mary at the Lord's feet; Martha called by name, not scolded.
Bethany: Martha's faith, Mary's tears and perfume, Lazarus raised.
Bethany Ashram and our own homes: welcome and prayer belong together.
live: Invite someone who is alone, a neighbour, a new family or a visitor to the parish, for tea or a meal this week.
Before the first task tomorrow, read the Gospel of the day for five minutes in silence and listen to what the Lord says to you.
Do one task at home today, with no complaint and a prayer, as done for the Lord.
2027-07-29.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, friend of Martha, Mary and Lazarus, you were welcomed into their home at Bethany and you wept at their grief. Come into our homes. Make us welcoming to every stranger, attentive to your word, and faithful in service. Teach us the one thing that is needed, that we may sit at your feet and rise to serve, and bring us at last to the house where there is no more death. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbono the two halves of Bethany meet: we sit first at the Lord's feet to listen to the Word, as Mary did, and then we are brought to his table, where he serves us himself with his own Body and Blood, and sends us out to serve.
conn: Hebrews 13:2 recalls Genesis 18, where Abraham says to the three travellers at Mamre: “My lord, if I find favor with you, do not pass by your servant.”
At the feet of the teacher.
Luke 10:39: Mary “sat at the Lord's feet”; Acts 22:3 shows Paul as “brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel”, the posture of a disciple.
John 11:27: “Yes, Lord, I believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God, the one coming into the world”: the active sister makes the great confession of faith, as Peter does at Caesarea Philippi.
fathers: Martha's task is good, but Mary's is better, for Martha's work will pass away with this life, while what Mary has chosen will not be taken from her; yet we are all both Martha and Mary, until we come to the home where we shall only rejoice in the Lord (Sermon 104, in substance).
Let all guests who arrive be received as Christ, for he himself will say: I was a stranger and you took me in (Rule 53, in substance).
magis: Jesus links faith in the resurrection to his own person: “I am the resurrection and the life”; Christ himself will raise up on the last day those who have believed in him (in substance).
The works of mercy are charitable actions by which we come to the aid of our neighbour in his spiritual and bodily needs; to welcome the stranger is among them (in substance).
Prayer and Christian life are inseparable, for they concern the same love and the same renunciation, which proceeds from love (in substance).

Jesus loved Martha, Mary and Lazarus of Bethany, and he raised Lazarus from the dead.
2027-07-29.action: Invite someone to your home this week, or call someone who is alone, and give them your full attention.
2027-07-29.question: When the Lord comes to my house, am I busy for him or with him?

family.explain: Martha, Mary and Lazarus were great friends of Jesus. They lived in a village called Bethany, and Jesus loved to visit their home. Martha cooked and worked hard, and Mary sat down beside Jesus to listen to him. Jesus loved them both. He wanted Martha to know that listening to him is the most important thing of all. When we welcome visitors and when we pray, we do what Martha and Mary did.
family.intention: We pray for everyone who has no home or no one to visit them.
family.ask: Ask: “How can we welcome someone to our house this week?”

illus: At a parish feast near Changanassery two women, sisters-in-law, kept the same roles for years. Annamma cooked for three hundred people and never sat in church for the sermon; Mariamma sat in the first pew every day and never entered the kitchen. Each privately believed the other had it wrong. When their old parish priest died, a note was found in his missal: “Annamma, sit in the front pew for once. Mariamma, take the ladle for a day.” They did it, rather stiffly, the next year, and afterwards they shared both. “I did not know what I had been missing,” Annamma said. Mariamma said, “I did not know how heavy the pot was.” The parish still tells it as the story of Bethany.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you were welcomed at Bethany. Come into our homes, and teach us to listen to you and to serve you with joy. Amen.
share: Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers (Hebrews 13:2). Whom could I welcome this week?
Martha, Martha, you are worried and distracted by many things (Luke 10:41). What is distracting me from the Lord?
Mary has chosen the better part (Luke 10:42). Where do I find time to sit at his feet?
pm.resp: Lord, come and stay in our house.
interc: For the Church, that she may be a home where every stranger is welcomed and every disciple listens to the Word.
For refugees, migrants and all who are far from their homes, that they may find a welcome.
For those who serve in kitchens, hospitals and homes without being seen, that their work may be given to the Lord.
For the communities of the Bethany Ashram and all who join prayer with work, that they may be faithful.
For the dying and the bereaved, that they may hear the Lord say: I am the resurrection and the life.
pm.close: Father, you gave your Son a home at Bethany among the friends he loved. Make us welcoming to him in the stranger, attentive to his word, and faithful in service, that at the last we may be welcomed into your house. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

term: In the Bible welcoming a stranger is a holy duty, not only a courtesy: Abraham welcomed three travellers at Mamre (Genesis 18), Hebrews 13:2 recalls this, and the Lord says that whoever welcomes the least of his brothers and sisters welcomes him (Matthew 25:35, 40). In the Syriac Churches the monasteries have always kept a guest house.
kidsaint: In a little village called Bethany lived a brother and two sisters: Lazarus, Martha and Mary. Jesus loved to visit their home. When he came, Martha hurried to cook a good meal, and Mary sat down at his feet to listen to every word. One day Lazarus became very sick and died, and everyone cried. Jesus came and cried too, because he loved his friend. Then he called out, “Lazarus, come out!” and Lazarus came out of the tomb alive. Lesson: Jesus is the best friend a family can have. Let us welcome him with a kind heart and listen to him.

homily: Dear friends, the Letter to the Hebrews tells us: Let mutual love continue. Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by doing that some have entertained angels without knowing it (Hebrews 13:1–2). Abraham ran out to three travellers at noon, and found that they were messengers of God. A home where love is steady and the stranger is welcome is a small Church.

In the Gospel a woman named Martha welcomed Jesus into her home. Let us not be unfair to her. She was the host. Her trouble was that she was worried and distracted by many things, while her sister Mary sat at the Lord's feet and listened. Jesus called her name twice, with great love: Martha, Martha. There is need of only one thing, and Mary has chosen the better part (Luke 10:41–42).

John tells us that Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. When Lazarus died, Martha ran to meet the Lord and made her great confession: I believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God (John 11:27). Mary fell at his feet; Jesus wept; Lazarus came out of the tomb. Martha serves, Mary anoints: the two are halves of one discipleship. Mary of Bethany is not Mary Magdalene.
So let us open our homes, and then sit at his feet. Let the day begin with five minutes of listening, and let our service be done without grumbling. At the Holy Qurbono he serves us himself. Amen.
kids: Children, do you like it when your friends come to your house? Jesus had friends called Martha, Mary and Lazarus, and he loved to visit them. Martha cooked, and Mary sat beside Jesus to listen to him. Jesus loved them both, but he wanted Martha to know that listening to him is the most important thing. Today, when someone comes to your home, say hello with a happy face. And before you do your homework, sit quietly for a moment and tell Jesus, “Welcome, Lord. I am listening.”
